title: Why Democrats Can’t Stop the DSA
author: Alex Hogan
content:
![Why Democrats Can’t Stop the
DSA](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/08/AP26213116741060.jpg)

The Democratic Socialists of America's hot socialist summer continues.
Although the election remains too close to call as of this writing, Abdul El-
Sayed looks likely to prevail in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary, adding
to a momentum that has been building for months. In June, a slate endorsed by
the organization's highest-profile elected official, New York City Mayor
Zohran Mamdani, defeated three incumbent Democrats in the state's
congressional primaries. DSA-backed candidates have also defeated
establishment Democrats in Colorado, Washington, DC, and Los Angeles,
underscoring the organization's growing clout. The winning streak isn't over.
In Wisconsin, DSA member Francesca Hong holds a comfortable lead ahead of this
month's Democratic primary for governor.

It is hardly surprising that the Democratic establishment is panicking. "The
DSA poses a fundamental threat to the Democratic Party and to the nation as a
whole," a former Clinton State Department official
[_told_](https://www.wsj.com/politics/elections/democratic-socialists-mamdani-
midterms-party-ca2ddf9a?ref=compactmag.com)  _The Wall Street Journal_.
Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville went further, arguing it is "time
for Democrats to talk the S-word: schism." _The Atlantic_ 's James Kirchick
described the DSA as a "parasite" and argued that Democratic leaders should
purge its supporters.

But no state Democratic Party--which is governed by state election law, not
party rules--has the authority to exclude anyone from registering to vote or
running in its primaries. And even if the DNC could somehow excise every DSA
member from the state voter rolls, it wouldn't stop the left-wing insurgency.
The DSA is growing because it has tapped into the frustration and alienation
felt by a significant segment of the Democratic coalition, particularly voters
under thirty-five.

Mamdani won roughly [ _75 percent_](https://circle.tufts.edu/latest-
research/young-voters-power-mamdani-victory-shape-
key-2025-elections?ref=compactmag.com) of voters under thirty last November,
while youth turnout reached about 28 percent of eligible voters, roughly 20
percent higher than in New York City's 2013 mayoral election. His endorsed
Congressional slate performed nearly as well. A [ _late July
poll_](https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/5997606-el-sayed-leads-stevens-
michigan-senate-poll/?ref=compactmag.com) found that voters under fifty
supported El-Sayed by 42 percentage points over his establishment-backed
opponent, Haley Stevens. The only age group in which Stevens led was of those
over sixty. In Wisconsin, [
_polling_](https://today.marquette.edu/2026/07/marquette-law-poll-finds-
expanded-support-for-hong-in-democratic-primary-barnes-sits-second-and-
crowley-third/?ref=compactmag.com) shows Francesca Hong pulling in similar
numbers, winning 66 percent of voters under twenty-nine, and 51 percent of
those under forty-four.

> "It is the message, more than any particular personality, that is driving
> their success."

Mamdani may be a once-in-a-generation political talent. But the fact that DSA
candidates across the country are attracting similar support from younger
voters suggests that it is the message, more than any particular personality,
that is driving their success. A recent Cato Institute [
_poll_](https://www.cato.org/blog/young-americans-socialism-too-much-thats-
problem-libertarians-must-fix?ref=compactmag.com) found that more than 60
percent of Americans aged 18-29 hold a favorable view of socialism.

It isn't easy to divine exactly what young voters mean by the term. As
pollster Rachel Janfaza [ _wrote on
X_](https://x.com/racheljanfaza/status/2082446327980441633?ref=compactmag.com):
"I've been asking Gen Z voters in our focus groups to define socialism, and
there's not a real consensus on what it actually means." But many, she found,
identify policies like paid family leave as "socialist"--in effect, amounting
to a more generous welfare state.

That young voters, especially those with a college degree, have soured on the
existing economy isn't surprising. For one thing, even as the cost of a degree
continues to rise, AI is creating enormous uncertainty about future job
security for newly degreed professionals. Inflation and especially rising
housing costs have made life hard for those just starting out. [ _A
poll_](https://iop.harvard.edu/youth-poll/52nd-edition-
spring-2026?ref=compactmag.com) by the Institute of Politics at Harvard
Kennedy School found that voters under twenty-nine see the rising cost of
living as a generational crisis.

This sense of economic distress is paired with historic levels of distrust in
politics as usual. The same Harvard poll shows that members of Congress
receive nearly identical approval ratings regardless of party, with only about
a quarter of Gen Z voters expressing support. On foreign policy, [_more than
half of voters_](https://news.gallup.com/poll/702440/israelis-no-longer-ahead-
americans-middle-east-sympathies.aspx?ref=compactmag.com) aged between
eighteen and thirty-four now sympathize more with Palestinians than Israelis.
Taken together, all of this discontent adds up to a political tinderbox that
was waiting for a spark.

Centrist Democrats, especially those concerned with winning in swing
districts, have legitimate reasons to be concerned about how the DSA's
increasing prominence will impact otherwise winnable statewide races, like
those in Michigan and Wisconsin. The DSA platform is full of nuggets that are
toxic to many working-class swing voters, from open borders to defunding the
police to racial reparations; same goes for the
[_rhetoric_](https://www.foxnews.com/video/6402289926112?ref=compactmag.com)
of some of the organization's leadership.

But as long as the DSA candidates are seen as a force for change by voters fed
up with the status quo, there is little party leaders can do to stop them.
Moreover, because electoral politics is about stitching together the widest
coalition possible, Democrats can't afford to write off what is now a large
segment of its electorate.

Some have analogized the rise of the DSA to the MAGA movement's takeover of
the Republican Party, and the parallels are real. Donald Trump identified a
critical segment of the Republican electorate that had become alienated from
the party establishment and focused relentlessly on issues that other
candidates were unwilling to address, chiefly immigration and trade.

While Trump and the DSA appeal to very different constituencies, both--like
populist movements more broadly--tap into a perceived loss of status among
their supporters. Trump's initial appeal was rooted in white blue-collar
voters who saw their cultural standing threatened by globalization and
increasingly racial and ethnic diversity. The DSA, by contrast, draws support
from college-educated voters confronting professional and economic
disappointment in an increasingly hostile economy. In both cases, that sense
of frustration and decline has turned them against the political
establishments of their own parties.

But while Trump was able to ride that wave to two historically narrow
political victories, a less forgiving Electoral College map means Democrats
must knit together a broader coalition to take back the presidency. Centrists
concerned about the party's electoral viability must thread a very fine
needle. They must address the grievances fueling the DSA's growth and
demonstrate a willingness to break with an out-of-touch party establishment
while maintaining enough independence from the left to appeal to the broader
electorate. Whether any politician has the skill to pull that off--or whether
the DSA will continue to fill the vacuum left by a crumbling Democratic center
--will largely determine the course of the 2028 campaign.
